title: Start with what we can observe
subtitle: Observations, models, and a prediction we can test
paragraphs: Suppose we learn that an object in space is approaching Earth. That gives us something to investigate, but it does not tell us where the object will arrive. Approaching Earth and hitting Earth are different claims. Our job is to use observations to build a prediction we can explain. In this unit, we will do that with our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ.

Find observation in Section A. An observation is something we record or measure. A position at a particular time is an observation. A prediction is an estimate of what comes next. To connect the two, we use a model: a useful description with an assumption. We might say, “If the motion keeps going the same way, this pattern will continue.” The word if matters because the next observation can test that assumption.

Look at the position dots in Section C. A cart is at 0 m, 2 m, and 4 m, with one second between measurements. Each second its position increases by 2 m. If the pattern continues, we predict 6 m at 3 s. The dashed outline marks a prediction, not another measurement. Blue identifies position. Purple identifies the motion pattern connecting those positions.

Section D uses a different cart. Its measured positions are 2 m, 3 m, and 4 m, again one second apart. First find what changes between readings: 3 m − 2 m = +1 m, and 4 m − 3 m = +1 m. The two changes agree. That gives us a reason to extend the pattern by one more second.

Our rule is <eq>next position = last position + change during the next second</eq>. Applying it gives <eq>4 m + 1 m = 5 m</eq>. I want the condition to stay with the answer: the prediction is 5 m if the motion continues the same way. If a new reading gives a different position, we should check the measurement and whether the cart changed its motion.

Three symbols will help us describe motion throughout the unit. Position, <var>x</var>, tells us where an object is relative to a chosen zero. Velocity, <var>v</var>, tells us how fast position changes and which way the object moves. Acceleration, <var>a</var>, tells us how velocity changes. These quantities answer different questions. We will learn how to connect them instead of treating every number as just “how fast.”

A testable question is one that measurements can help answer. “Where will it be tomorrow?” is testable once we have enough information and a model. “Who should pay for a mission?” also involves human priorities and decisions. Physics can inform those decisions, but a calculation alone cannot make them.

For 2026-XJ, we will need positions, times, directions, and information about how reliable the measurements are. Later, forces will help us explain changes in its motion. The question tying that work together is the one on your notes page: how fast is it moving, and where will it arrive?

title: Where you finish is not the whole trip
subtitle: Position, distance, and displacement
paragraphs: If I say a cart is at two meters, you need to know where we started measuring. Position needs a chosen zero, called the origin. We also choose a positive direction. On today's notes page, right is positive. Once those choices are clear, a position tells us where the cart is along the line.

Position is a location. Distance counts how much travel occurred. Displacement describes the change from starting position to final position. Those are three different questions, so one trip can have three different descriptions. I want you to decide which question is being asked before calculating anything.

Trace both legs in Section C. It shows a trip from 0 m to 4 m, then back to 1 m. The outward leg is four meters long. The return leg is three meters long. Total distance is distance = 4 m + 3 m = 7 m. Coming back does not erase the first leg. Distance counts every part of the route and is never negative.

Displacement uses only the starting and finishing positions. The symbol Δ means “change in,” so Δ<var>x</var> means change in position. The rule is <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>x</var><sub>f</sub> − <var>x</var><sub>i</sub></eq>: finish minus start. For the diagram, <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = 1 m − 0 m = +1 m</eq>. The cart finishes one meter right of where it began, even though it traveled seven meters.

Now find the starting and turning positions in Section D. The cart starts at 2 m, travels to 6 m, and returns to 4 m. Its first leg is 6 m − 2 m = 4 m. The return leg has length 6 m − 4 m = 2 m. Add the lengths to find distance = 4 m + 2 m = 6 m. The direction of a leg does not make its length negative.

For displacement, use the endpoints instead: <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = 4 m − 2 m = +2 m</eq>. The final position is 4 m from our chosen zero, while the displacement is 2 m right of the starting point. Those answers differ because the cart did not start at zero. This is a common place to lose track of what a number means.

Distance is a scalar: it has size and units. Displacement is a vector: it also has direction. Along one axis, the sign gives that direction. A negative displacement would mean a finish left of the start. In the diagram, the traveled route stays in pencil; the positions and displacement arrow are blue.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we need the same clear reference frame. Measuring from Earth gives our classroom model a zero, but we must still name the positive direction. Total distance describes the route traveled. Starting position and displacement tell us where the asteroid ends up. That is the information a position forecast needs.

title: Read motion from the slope
subtitle: Velocity, speed, and position-time graphs
paragraphs: A position tells us where an object is. To describe its motion, we need to know how that position changes over time. Moving six meters in three seconds and moving six meters in thirty seconds are different motions. Velocity combines the position change, the elapsed time, and the direction.

Use the average-velocity equation in Section B: v = Δx ÷ Δt. The units are meters per second, or m/s. Average speed uses total distance divided by elapsed time. Speed has no direction and cannot be negative. When a trip includes a return, average speed and the size of average velocity can be different because distance and displacement are different.

A position-time graph places time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis. Its height tells us position. Its slope tells us velocity. Slope means rise divided by run: the change in position divided by the change in time. A rising line means motion in the positive direction. A falling line means motion in the negative direction.

Follow the rising, flat, and falling parts of the graph in Section C. From 0 s to 2 s, position rises from 0 m to 4 m. The slope is 4 m ÷ 2 s = +2 m/s. From 2 s to 4 s, position stays at 4 m. The flat line has zero slope, so the object is stopped. From 4 s to 6 s, it returns to 0 m, giving −4 m ÷ 2 s = −2 m/s.

The return slope is negative, but its size matches the first slope. The object moves at the same speed in the opposite direction. A steeper position-time line would mean a greater speed. The graph is not a picture of a hill or road. Its shape records how position changes as time passes. The purple marks connect those slopes with velocity.

In Section D, the cart goes from 8 m to 2 m in 3 s. Right is positive. First find displacement: Δx = 2 m − 8 m = −6 m. Then divide by time: v = −6 m ÷ 3 s = −2 m/s. That means an average velocity of two meters per second to the left. The minus sign gives direction, not a negative speed.

The notes also give a useful unit conversion: <eq>1 m/s = 3.6 km/h</eq>. A speed of 2 m/s is therefore <eq>(2)(3.6) = 7.2 km/h</eq>. Changing units changes the number used to describe the motion, not the motion itself.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, measured positions and their times let us estimate velocity. In the lab, the same idea applies to your cart: use the actual graph and its labeled axes. I want the slope calculation and your description of direction to tell the same story.

title: Read the axes before you read the line
subtitle: Velocity-time graphs, signed area, and components
paragraphs: A flat line does not always mean an object is stopped. On yesterday's position-time graph, a flat line meant position stayed the same. On today's velocity-time graph, it means velocity stays the same. I want the axis labels to be the first thing you read. They tell you what the line's height actually represents.

If the line stays at +2 m/s, the object keeps moving in the positive direction at two meters per second. If it stays at −1 m/s, the object keeps moving in the negative direction at one meter per second. Only a line at zero velocity describes an object remaining stopped. A negative velocity is a direction, not automatically slowing motion.

The area between a velocity line and the time axis gives displacement. For a constant velocity, that area is a rectangle. Its height is velocity and its width is elapsed time, so <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>v</var> × <var>t</var></eq>. Multiplying meters per second by seconds leaves meters, the unit for a change in position.

Find the time axis on both graphs in Section C. The first graph shows +2 m/s for 4 s. Its area gives Δx = (2 m/s)(4 s) = +8 m. The second shows −1 m/s for 4 s, giving Δx = (−1 m/s)(4 s) = −4 m. Area above zero adds positive displacement. Area below zero adds negative displacement. The blue regions represent those position changes, while the velocity lines are purple.

The example in Section D uses +3 m/s for 2 s. Apply the same rule: Δx = (3 m/s)(2 s) = +6 m. With right chosen as positive, the cart ends six meters right of where it began. This is displacement, not its final coordinate. To find the final coordinate, we would also need the starting position.

A velocity arrow can point diagonally rather than along one axis. We then describe it with two components: a horizontal part and a vertical part. For an angle θ measured from the positive horizontal axis, <eq><var>v</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>v</var> cos <var>θ</var></eq> and <eq><var>v</var><sub>y</sub> = <var>v</var> sin <var>θ</var></eq>. Cosine finds the part next to that angle; sine finds the opposite part. Both components describe the same motion happening at the same time.

For example, a 10 m/s velocity at 30° above that axis has components <eq><var>v</var><sub>x</sub> = 10 cos 30° ≈ 8.66 m/s</eq> and <eq><var>v</var><sub>y</sub> = 10 sin 30° = 5 m/s</eq>. Use degree mode and check the arrow's direction before assigning signs.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, the velocity graph shows how motion changes with time. Components show how much motion is toward Earth and how much is sideways. We need both pieces to predict a path, rather than assuming that all of its speed carries it directly toward us.

title: Start with the starting position
subtitle: Steady-velocity predictions and their possible range
paragraphs: Imagine a cart already sitting at the eight-meter mark. If it moves six meters left, it does not finish at negative six meters. Negative six meters describes its change in position. We still have to combine that change with where the cart started. Today I want you to keep those two steps visible.

For steady velocity, the position change is velocity times elapsed time. Final position is starting position plus that change: <eq><var>x</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>x</var><sub>0</sub> + <var>v</var><var>t</var></eq>. The subscript zero identifies the position when our chosen time interval begins. The starting position can be positive, negative, or zero. We should copy it from the situation, not assume it.

Find the starting dot and the displacement arrow in Section C. The trip begins at 2 m and shows motion at +2 m/s for 3 s. First calculate change = (2 m/s)(3 s) = +6 m. Then xf = 2 m + 6 m = 8 m. The dot marks the starting position, and the blue arrow marks the change. The answer is a coordinate measured from the same zero used at the start.

In Section D, the cart starts at 8 m and moves at −2 m/s for 3 s. The negative velocity means motion left when right is positive. Its change is (−2 m/s)(3 s) = −6 m. Add that signed change to the start: xf = 8 m + (−6 m) = 2 m. The final position remains positive even though the cart moved in the negative direction.

Measurements also have limits. A prediction written as 8 ± 1 m means a central value of 8 m with an allowed range from 7 m to 9 m. The plus-or-minus amount extends to each side of the center. It is not the full width. Here the full interval is two meters wide, as the shaded region shows.

For steady velocity and an exact elapsed time, we can use a conservative bound: <eq>largest position error = start error + velocity error × time</eq>. If the starting error is 0.5 m and velocity error is 0.1 m/s, after three seconds the bound is <eq>0.5 m + (0.1 m/s)(3 s) = 0.8 m</eq>. More elapsed time lets the velocity uncertainty build into more position uncertainty. This range does not state an impact probability.

Check units before multiplying. If velocity is in meters per second, time needs to be in seconds: <eq>2 h = 7,200 s</eq>. In two dimensions, apply the same start-plus-change idea separately to the vertical coordinate: <eq><var>y</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>y</var><sub>0</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>y</sub><var>t</var></eq>.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a responsible forecast includes the future time, predicted location, range, and steady-motion assumption. If its velocity changes, we need to revise the model rather than trust a precise-looking answer from the wrong equation.

title: Keep direction attached to every arrow
subtitle: Tip-to-tail addition and splitting vectors into parts
paragraphs: An arrow gives us two pieces of information: size and direction. Together they describe a vector. Displacement, velocity, and force are vectors, so their directions must stay attached when we combine them. Adding only the arrow lengths can give the wrong result when the arrows point different ways.

Follow the arrows tip to tail in Section C. They show displacement A going 4 m east and 1 m north, followed by displacement B going 2 m west and 2 m north. To add them visually, place the tail of B at the tip of A. Keep each arrow's length and direction unchanged. The resultant is the arrow from the first starting point to the final endpoint.

We can check that picture by adding components. Take east and north as positive. Horizontally, <eq><var>R</var><sub>x</sub> = 4 m − 2 m = 2 m</eq> east. Vertically, <eq><var>R</var><sub>y</sub> = 1 m + 2 m = 3 m</eq> north. In symbols, <eq><var>R</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>A</var><sub>x</sub> + <var>B</var><sub>x</sub></eq> and <eq><var>R</var><sub>y</sub> = <var>A</var><sub>y</sub> + <var>B</var><sub>y</sub></eq>. Add horizontal parts together and vertical parts together.

Those perpendicular parts form a right triangle. The resultant's size is <eq>|<var>R</var>| = √[(2 m)² + (3 m)²] ≈ 3.61 m</eq>. Its angle from the positive horizontal direction is <eq><var>θ</var> = tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 2) ≈ 56.3°</eq>, toward north from east. Check both signs before interpreting an angle. The arrow here must point right and up because both components are positive.

We can also work backward, splitting one diagonal arrow into its parts. The force example in Section D gives a 20 N force at 30° above the positive horizontal axis. The horizontal part is next to the angle, so use cosine: Fx = F cos θ = (20 N) cos 30° ≈ 17.3 N. The vertical part is opposite, so Fy = F sin θ = (20 N) sin 30° = 10.0 N.

Both force components are positive in this example. Use degree mode, and name the axis from which the angle is measured. If the angle begins at another axis, identify the adjacent and opposite parts again. I want the sketch to guide the sine-or-cosine choice.

The 17.3 N and 10.0 N values describe parts of one 20 N force. They are not two new forces to add on top of it. Similarly, the blue displacement components describe one overall change in position. Components organize the calculation without creating extra motion or extra interactions.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, motion has parts in more than one direction. Adding vectors keeps those directions in the prediction. Splitting a velocity arrow helps us distinguish motion toward Earth from motion across our line of sight.

title: Acceleration means velocity is changing
subtitle: Reading dot patterns and calculating change each second
paragraphs: We often use the word accelerate to mean speed up, but in physics it has a wider meaning. Acceleration is a change in velocity over time. Speeding up is one example. Slowing down and turning are examples too, because velocity includes both speed and direction. I want us to describe the change before deciding what the acceleration means.

The calculation is <eq><var>a</var> = Δ<var>v</var> ÷ Δ<var>t</var></eq>. First subtract starting velocity from final velocity. Then divide by elapsed time. The unit m/s² means meters per second, each second. An acceleration of 2 m/s² means velocity changes by two meters per second during each second if the acceleration stays constant.

The cart in Section D starts at 0 m/s and reaches 8 m/s in 4 s. The velocity change is Δv = 8 m/s − 0 m/s = 8 m/s. Divide by the time: a = 8 m/s ÷ 4 s = 2 m/s². That is the average acceleration over the interval. With steady acceleration, the velocities at successive whole seconds would be 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 m/s.

The second equation in Section B gives v = v0 + at. This says final velocity equals starting velocity plus the change built up over time. For our steady-acceleration example, v = 0 m/s + (2 m/s²)(4 s) = 8 m/s. The two equations describe the same change from different starting information.

Compare the gaps between dots in the three rows of Section C. They mark position at equal time intervals. Growing gaps mean the object travels farther during each interval, so it speeds up. Shrinking gaps mean it travels less during each interval, so it slows down. Equal gaps along a straight path mean steady velocity and zero acceleration. Green, red, and yellow mark those three patterns on the notes page.

A negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. Along a straight line, compare the signs of velocity and acceleration. When they have the same sign, speed grows. When they have opposite signs, speed decreases until a possible turn. A cart moving right can slow under leftward acceleration; a cart already moving left can speed up under that same acceleration.

Turning matters too. An object going around a curve at steady speed still changes its direction, so its velocity changes and it accelerates. Near Earth's surface, free fall is another example: ignoring air resistance, gravity produces about 9.8 m/s² downward. The sign depends on which direction we choose as positive.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, changing velocity readings tell us that a steady-velocity forecast may need revision. The important question is how much velocity changes, over what time, and in which direction. That information lets us begin explaining a changing path instead of simply extending an old pattern.

title: Choose a motion model before an equation
subtitle: Steady acceleration and displacement from average velocity
paragraphs: A cart traveling steadily at 8 m/s for four seconds covers a different distance from a cart that starts at rest and only reaches 8 m/s at the end. Using the final velocity for the whole interval would pretend the second cart was already moving that fast at the start. Today I want the equation to match the actual motion.

Steady velocity means velocity does not change. In that case, <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>v</var><var>t</var></eq>. Constant acceleration means velocity changes by the same amount each second. For constant acceleration, the average velocity is <eq><var>v</var><sub>avg</sub> = (<var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>f</sub>) ÷ 2</eq>. Averaging only the starting and ending velocities works because the change between them is steady.

The cart in Section D speeds up steadily from 0 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s. First find the average: vavg = (0 + 8) m/s ÷ 2 = 4 m/s. Then multiply by elapsed time: Δx = (4 m/s)(4 s) = +16 m. The cart's position changes sixteen meters in the positive direction.

We can combine those steps into <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = ½(<var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>f</sub>)<var>t</var></eq>. The one-half simply tells us to divide the sum of the endpoint velocities by two. The result is displacement. If the object reversed direction during another problem, we would need to distinguish that signed change from the total distance traveled.

Trace the triangle and the dashed rectangle in Section C. This graph uses a smaller final velocity: 0 to 4 m/s in 4 s. The straight rising line shows constant acceleration. Its triangular area is ½(4 s)(4 m/s) = 8 m. The average-velocity rectangle has height 2 m/s and the same width, giving (2 m/s)(4 s) = 8 m. Different shapes give the same area and therefore the same displacement.

The constant-acceleration equations in Section B connect other sets of known values. v = v0 + at finds velocity from its starting value, acceleration, and time. Δx = v0t + ½at² finds displacement from those quantities. v² = v0² + 2aΔx is useful when time is not given or needed.

Start by listing the given values with units and naming what is asked. Then choose a relationship that uses that information and fits the model. Finish by checking the units and signs. A calculation for displacement should end in meters, and its sign should agree with the motion. Do not assume constant acceleration just because an equation is available.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, choosing steady velocity or steady acceleration is a decision about the evidence. I want the reason for that choice to travel with the predicted position. A correct substitution cannot rescue a model that does not fit the motion.

title: Moving does not require an unbalanced force
subtitle: Newton's first law, balanced forces, and inertia
paragraphs: A cart moving across a rough floor slows down after we stop pushing. It is easy to conclude that every moving object needs a forward force to keep going. But the cart is still interacting with the floor and air. We need to identify those forces before deciding what motion would look like without them.

A force is a push or pull from an interaction. The net force is the combined effect of all the forces on one object. Newton's first law says an object keeps its velocity unless a nonzero net force changes it. If the object is at rest, it stays at rest. If it is already moving, it continues at constant speed in a straight line.

This rule applies in an inertial frame: a reference frame that is not itself accelerating or turning. We treat the classroom as such a frame for these examples. The key relationship is <eq>Σ<var>F</var> = 0</eq>, which gives <eq><var>a</var> = 0</eq> and unchanged velocity. The symbol Σ means add the forces, including their directions.

Compare the two horizontal arrows on the moving cart in Section C. A 4 N pull right balances 4 N of friction left. A 10 N normal force up balances 10 N of weight down. Each direction balances, so the cart has zero acceleration. It can still keep rolling right. The purple velocity arrow describes that motion and is not another force to add to the orange force arrows.

Inertia is an object's resistance to a change in velocity. More mass means more inertia. It is not a hidden forward force. A moving object does not need an additional “inertia arrow” in its force diagram. We use forces to explain changes in motion, rather than inventing a force merely because something is moving.

Now compare that cart with the one in Section D: a cart rolls right and slows down. Its velocity is changing, so its acceleration is not zero. The change points left, opposite the rightward motion. Therefore its net horizontal force must point left. Friction could cause that imbalance, but the observed motion alone tells us the net direction, not the exact size of each individual force.

If someone keeps pulling the cart right with a force equal to the backward friction, the forces balance and the cart can move steadily. If the pull becomes smaller than friction, the cart slows while moving right. This is why “there is a force” and “there is a net force” are different statements. Several forces can act and still add to zero.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, there is no need for a forward push simply to maintain its motion. Gravity can still change its velocity and bend its path. I want us to distinguish motion that continues because of inertia from motion that changes because of a net external force.

title: Name what is doing the pushing or pulling
subtitle: Force sources, contact forces, mass, and weight
paragraphs: A force arrow should tell us about an interaction, not just point in a direction that looks useful. I want you to be able to finish this sentence for every arrow: “The ___ exerts a ___ force on the object.” The first blank identifies the source. The object receiving the force is the receiver.

Some forces require contact. A normal force is a surface's push perpendicular to the surface. Friction acts along the contact surface and opposes slipping or the tendency to slip. Tension is a taut rope's pull along the rope. An applied force can be a person's push or pull. These names describe how objects interact.

Gravity can act without contact. Near Earth's surface, Earth pulls objects downward. We call the size of that gravitational force weight. Mass describes how much matter an object has and is measured in kilograms. Weight is a force and is measured in newtons. A three-kilogram object does not have a weight of three kilograms; those units describe its mass.

Use the weight equation in Section B: W = mg, also written using gravitational force as Fg = mg. Near Earth, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg. That means each kilogram has about 9.8 N of gravitational force acting on it. For estimates and today's worked example, the notes round this to 10 N/kg.

The worked example places a 3 kg object at rest on a level table. Its estimated weight is W = (3 kg)(10 N/kg) = 30 N downward. The table supplies an upward normal force. Because the object remains at rest and there are no other vertical forces in this example, the normal force must also be 30 N. Equal upward and downward forces give zero vertical acceleration.

Name the source of each of the four force arrows on the crate in Section C. The rope pulls right with 6 N of tension. The table supplies 2 N of backward friction and 10 N of upward normal force. Earth supplies 10 N of downward weight. One source, the table, can supply two different contact forces. The vertical forces balance, while the horizontal forces have a net effect to the right.

Normal force is not automatically equal to weight. That equality followed from the level-table situation with no other vertical pull and no vertical acceleration. A ramp or another supporting force can change it. Similarly, a velocity arrow is not a force source. “It is moving” cannot fill in the first blank of our interaction sentence.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, naming sources helps us decide which forces belong in its model. Gravity from other bodies can change its motion without contact. A rope or table force belongs only if such an interaction exists. A complete, realistic force list is the starting point for explaining a changing path.

title: Change the mass and watch the acceleration
subtitle: A fair test with the same net force
paragraphs: Imagine pushing an empty cart and then the same cart loaded with more mass. With the same net force, the loaded cart changes velocity more slowly. Today's lab tests that relationship. I want the evidence to come from measured motion, with the force conditions kept as consistent as possible.

A fair test changes one intended quantity at a time. Here that quantity is the total moving mass. In our cart-and-hanger system, count the cart, added masses, and hanger if all of them move as part of the system. Leaving out part of the moving mass would make the comparison incomplete.

Keep the hanging mass, track, starting point, and release method consistent as the notes describe. Releasing without an extra push matters because a different starting motion could change the trial. Holding the hanging mass steady keeps the driving pull similar. Friction and other resistance still need attention because the relationship we want concerns the net force, not merely the hanging weight.

Use the two velocities and elapsed time in Section D. We find acceleration from the slope of each velocity-time graph: a = Δv ÷ Δt. In the worked example, velocity rises from 0 m/s to 4 m/s in 2 s. First find Δv = 4 m/s − 0 m/s = 4 m/s. Then a = 4 m/s ÷ 2 s = 2 m/s². Your experiment uses your own measured graph, not these example readings.

Compare the three masses in Section C. The picture gives illustrative values for a fixed 4 N net force. A 1 kg system accelerates at 4 m/s², a 2 kg system at 2 m/s², and a 4 kg system at 1 m/s². Doubling mass halves acceleration when the net force stays the same. This is an inverse relationship: as mass increases, acceleration decreases in that particular way.

Another check is the product of mass and acceleration. The examples give <eq>(1 kg)(4 m/s²) = 4 N</eq>, <eq>(2 kg)(2 m/s²) = 4 N</eq>, and <eq>(4 kg)(1 m/s²) = 4 N</eq>. Each product is the same because the net force is the same. Real measurements may not match perfectly, so look for a pattern while considering measurement uncertainty and changes in resistance.

I want a conclusion to name both parts of the comparison: increasing total mass reduces acceleration under the same net force. Saying only “more mass means less acceleration” leaves out the condition. If the force changes too, we cannot predict the result from mass alone. The green acceleration arrows in the diagram show the relative sizes in the illustrated speeding-up cases.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, mass matters when considering a proposed push. The same net push has less effect on a larger mass. But gravity's force can also change with mass, so we should not use today's fixed-force comparison to claim that all heavier objects fall more slowly. We must keep track of what is actually being held constant.

title: Keep the mass fixed and change the force
subtitle: A proportional relationship and Newton's second law
paragraphs: Yesterday we changed mass while trying to keep the net force fixed. Today we reverse that comparison. We keep the total moving mass the same and change the force that drives the motion. Looking at both tests helps us see how force, mass, and acceleration fit together.

In the cart-and-hanger setup, moving masses from the cart to the hanger can increase the hanging weight while keeping total moving mass unchanged. We do not add new masses to the whole system during this comparison. The cart and hanger are both included in the total. That system boundary is what makes “same mass” a meaningful claim.

For a fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to net force. Proportional means that multiplying the net force by a factor multiplies acceleration by that same factor. Doubling the net force doubles acceleration. Tripling it triples acceleration. This comparison assumes that mass stays fixed and that we have correctly included opposing forces.

The ideal 2 kg system in Section C accelerates at 1 m/s² under 2 N, at 2 m/s² under 4 N, and at 3 m/s² under 6 N. These points form a straight line through zero on an acceleration-versus-net-force graph. Zero net force gives zero acceleration. It does not necessarily mean zero velocity.

The example in Section D begins with 2 N producing 1 m/s² and asks what happens at 4 N. Compare the forces: 4 N ÷ 2 N = 2. The force doubled, so new acceleration = 2 × 1 m/s² = 2 m/s². We can check with a = Fnet ÷ m = 4 N ÷ 2 kg = 2 m/s².

This combines the two lab patterns into Newton's second law: Fnet = ma. Acceleration increases with net force and decreases with mass when the other quantity is fixed. On the graph of acceleration against net force, slope is slope = 1/m. For 2 kg, that slope is 0.5 m/s² per newton: every additional newton adds half a meter per second of velocity change each second.

Real data may sit below the ideal line when plotted against the driving pull because friction reduces the net force. A bigger hanging weight is not automatically the same as a bigger net force by the same ratio. I want us to distinguish the pull we supply from the combined effect of all external forces. Use measured graph slopes for acceleration and describe the limits of the experiment.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, this relationship lets us connect a proposed net push with a predicted acceleration. Knowing the mass and net force gives us a reasoned estimate of how its velocity would change. The prediction is only as sound as the force information and assumptions going into it.

title: Find the net force before dividing by mass
subtitle: Using Newton's second law with opposing forces
paragraphs: A strong pull does not act alone when friction is also present. To predict acceleration, we need the combined effect of all the forces on the object. Newton's second law uses net force. I want that force sum to appear before the division by mass, so the calculation shows which interactions were included.

Choose an axis and a positive direction. With right positive, a rightward force enters the sum as positive and a leftward force as negative. Along the horizontal axis, <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>m</var><var>a</var><sub>x</sub></eq>. The symbol Σ means sum. For two opposing forces, this becomes <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>F</var><sub>right</sub> − <var>F</var><sub>left</sub></eq>.

Compare the horizontal arrows in Section C. They act on a 2 kg cart pulled right by 6 N, with 2 N of friction left. Its horizontal net force is 6 N − 2 N = 4 N right. The 20 N upward normal force balances the 20 N downward weight. Those vertical forces do not contribute to the horizontal sum, and their own vertical sum is zero.

The thick net-force arrow summarizes the two horizontal forces. It is not an additional interaction to add again. If we counted the pull, friction, and net-force arrow as three separate forces, we would count the same imbalance twice. The diagram and force equation are two ways to describe the same situation.

The example in Section D uses a 4 kg cart, a 12 N pull right, and 4 N of friction left. First combine the forces: Fnet = 12 N − 4 N = +8 N. Then use a = Fnet ÷ m, giving a = 8 N ÷ 4 kg = 2 m/s² right. Dividing 12 N by 4 kg would ignore friction.

Acceleration points in the direction of the net force. Its size tells us the velocity change each second. The unit check agrees: <eq>1 N = 1 kg·m/s²</eq>, so newtons divided by kilograms give m/s². We can also check backward: <eq>(4 kg)(2 m/s²) = 8 N</eq>, matching the net force we found.

A rightward acceleration does not prove the cart is moving right. If it already moves right, it speeds up. If it moves left, it initially slows down. We need its starting velocity to describe that part of the motion. If the forces balance, acceleration is zero; the cart can remain still or keep a constant velocity.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, mass and net force determine acceleration. Then the existing velocity and elapsed time tell us how that acceleration changes the motion. A careful force sum is the first link in that chain. It keeps a missing or double-counted interaction from changing the entire forecast.

title: A force pair belongs to two different objects
subtitle: Newton's third law and the receiver of each force
paragraphs: When you push on a wall, the wall pushes on you at the same time. These two forces come from one interaction. Newton's third law says the forces have equal sizes and opposite directions. The detail I want you to notice is where they act: your push acts on the wall, and the wall's push acts on you.

We can name a pair by swapping the two objects. If A pushes B, B pushes A. The relationship is <eq><var>F</var><sub>A on B</sub> = −<var>F</var><sub>B on A</sub></eq>. The minus sign means opposite directions. The force type is the same for both members of a pair. This is not a delay in which one force happens first and the partner follows later.

Find which cart receives each arrow in Section C. There, cart A has mass 1 kg and cart B has mass 3 kg. Their interaction pushes A left with 6 N and B right with 6 N. The equal-length orange arrows show equal force sizes. One arrow belongs to A and the other belongs to B. Putting both on A's diagram would describe the wrong receivers.

Equal force sizes do not mean equal accelerations. If these are the only horizontal forces, A has an acceleration of <eq>6 N ÷ 1 kg = 6 m/s²</eq> left. B has <eq>6 N ÷ 3 kg = 2 m/s²</eq> right. The smaller mass changes velocity more quickly under the same force size. The different effects do not change the equality of the interaction forces.

The apple example in Section D asks for the partner of Earth's downward gravitational pull on an apple. Swap the names: the apple pulls gravitationally on Earth. Earth receives that partner force, directed toward the apple. Near the apple, that is upward. Earth's much larger mass means its acceleration from this interaction is extremely small compared with the apple's.

The pair does not cancel in the force sum for the apple, because only one member acts on the apple. That is the meaning of the notes' reminder that pair forces never cancel on one object. If we choose a combined system containing both objects, the pair is internal and cancels in the combined force sum. The individual objects can still accelerate relative to each other.

Also, two balanced forces on one object are not automatically a third-law pair. Weight downward and table support upward both act on a resting book. Their partners are the book's pull on Earth and the book's push on the table. Naming the source and receiver separates an interaction pair from forces that happen to balance.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, Earth and the asteroid pull on each other equally. Their masses differ, so their accelerations differ. I want each force placed on the correct object's diagram before we use it to explain a change in motion.

title: Draw only the forces on your chosen object
subtitle: A clear free-body diagram and balanced lamp forces
paragraphs: A free-body diagram is a simple picture of the forces acting on one chosen object. It does not need to show every detail of the scene. In fact, leaving out extra detail helps us see the interactions. Begin by deciding which object is receiving all the forces you will draw.

Use the six drawing rules in Section B. Replace that object with a dot or simple box. List its interactions, then draw one arrow for each force. Each arrow points in the force's direction. Its length shows the force's relative strength, using one consistent scale. Label the arrow with the force name or symbol and be able to name its source. That is the choose, list, draw routine on your notes page.

The box in Section C is pulled right by a rope across a rough level floor. The rope supplies rightward tension. The floor supplies leftward friction and upward normal force. Earth supplies downward weight. All four forces act on the box. The floor can supply two different contact forces because normal force and friction describe different parts of the interaction.

There is no separate “motion force.” Motion describes what the box is doing; it is not another object pushing or pulling it. Today's force diagram therefore leaves velocity off. A velocity arrow can be shown in a separate motion sketch when useful, but it must not be mistaken for an extra force. The orange arrows are reserved for the interactions.

In Section D, a lamp with 20 N of weight hangs at rest from one vertical rope. Choose the lamp as the object. Earth pulls down with 20 N, and the rope pulls up with tension. There are two forces on the lamp in this model. Its being at rest does not mean no forces act.

Because the lamp remains at rest, vertical acceleration is zero and the forces balance. Choose up as positive. Then <eq><var>T</var> − 20 N = 0</eq>, so <eq><var>T</var> = 20 N</eq>. Draw equal-length arrows: 20 N down for weight and 20 N up for tension. Their sum is zero, matching the unchanged motion.

Those balanced forces are not a third-law pair. Both act on the lamp, while the partners act on different receivers: the lamp pulls on Earth and on the rope. Those partner forces belong on diagrams for Earth and the rope. Also, the net force is the sum of the two arrows, not a third arrow representing a new interaction.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we use the same method: choose the asteroid, identify the bodies interacting with it, and draw the forces on it. A clear diagram makes it easier to spot a missing force or an arrow that belongs to another object. That is how a simple sketch supports a reliable calculation.

title: Use the force diagram to find acceleration
subtitle: Ramp directions, weight components, and net force
paragraphs: On a level table, normal force points up and weight points down. On a ramp, the normal force tilts with the surface, but weight still points straight down toward Earth. I want us to keep the physical force directions clear before choosing axes for the calculation.

A useful choice is a positive axis downhill along the ramp and a second positive axis straight out from the surface. These axes match the block's allowed motion and the direction of the normal force. Choosing tilted axes does not tilt gravity. It changes how we describe the parts of that same downward force.

Weight has a component along the ramp and a component into the ramp. If the ramp is at angle θ above horizontal, the downhill component has size <eq><var>m</var><var>g</var> sin <var>θ</var></eq>, and the inward component has size <eq><var>m</var><var>g</var> cos <var>θ</var></eq>. These are parts of weight, not additional interactions. We can use the parts instead of the full weight when adding forces along the tilted axes.

Follow the arrows in Section C. They show weight downward, normal force outward from the ramp, and friction uphill. It also shows the downhill part of weight with a dashed arrow. That dashed arrow helps with the calculation. Do not count both the full weight and its components as separate forces, or weight would be included twice.

In Section D, the downhill weight component is already given as 7 N. Friction acts uphill with 3 N, and the block has mass 2 kg. Because the component is supplied, no trigonometry is needed to solve this example. With downhill positive, Fnet = 7 N − 3 N = +4 N along the ramp.

Now apply Newton's second law: <eq><var>a</var> = <var>F</var><sub>net</sub> ÷ <var>m</var> = 4 N ÷ 2 kg = 2 m/s²</eq> downhill. The direction matches the net force. If the block is already moving downhill, it speeds up. If it is moving uphill, the same downhill acceleration would initially slow that motion. Acceleration direction and current velocity direction are different pieces of information.

We also check the direction perpendicular to the ramp. For a block staying in contact with a straight ramp, there is no acceleration through the surface. If weight and normal force are the only forces with perpendicular components, the normal force balances the inward part of weight. It does not have to equal the whole weight. In general, we use <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>m</var><var>a</var><sub>x</sub></eq> and <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>y</sub> = <var>m</var><var>a</var><sub>y</sub></eq> for the two chosen axes.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a force diagram likewise gives the net force and acceleration direction. The existing velocity still matters when describing the resulting path. Useful axes simplify the calculation, while a clear distinction between actual forces and components keeps the model consistent.

title: Friction adjusts before sliding begins
subtitle: Static friction, its limit, and kinetic friction
paragraphs: A gentle push on a crate may leave it at rest. A stronger push may still leave it at rest. That does not mean the pushing force disappeared. Static friction can adjust to balance the pull, up to a limit. Today I want us to decide whether the surfaces are sliding before choosing a friction value.

Static friction acts when the contact surfaces are not slipping relative to each other. In the simple horizontal example, it matches the pull while the crate remains at rest. If the pull is 2 N, static friction can be 2 N backward. If the pull rises to 5 N, it can rise to 5 N, provided the maximum available friction has not been exceeded.

Find where the rising line stops in Section C. The graph uses a 6 N static-friction limit. The rising line shows friction matching the pull up to that limit. A pull greater than the limit cannot be balanced by static friction in this example, so sliding begins. The 6 N value is the greatest available static friction, not the friction that acts during every smaller pull.

During sliding, we use kinetic friction. The illustrative crate has 4 N of kinetic friction, shown by the lower horizontal part of the graph. The friction value changes because the contact is in a different state. We should not continue using the maximum static value after the crate is sliding.

The example in Section D gives a 2 kg crate sliding right, a 10 N pull right, and 4 N of kinetic friction left. First find the net force: Fnet = 10 N − 4 N = 6 N right. Then a = Fnet ÷ m = 6 N ÷ 2 kg = 3 m/s² right. The crate is moving right and accelerating right, so it speeds up.

Sometimes kinetic friction is not given directly. If a coefficient μ and normal force are supplied, use <eq><var>f</var><sub>k</sub> = <var>μ</var><var>F</var><sub>N</sub></eq>. The coefficient has no unit, so the answer has the same force unit as the normal force: newtons. For instance, a coefficient of 0.20 with a 20 N normal force would give <eq>(0.20)(20 N) = 4 N</eq>. Find the normal force from the situation rather than assuming a value.

Friction opposes slipping, or the tendency to slip, at the contact. Its direction must follow that contact behavior. It is not a rule that friction always points opposite an object's overall motion in every possible situation. A shoe can receive forward static friction from the ground while a person walks forward.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, there is no rubbing surface in empty space to apply this kind of friction. Gravity can still change its speed or direction, and atmospheric drag would be a different interaction inside an atmosphere. I want us to include the forces whose sources are actually present.

title: Find what is needed to make the forces balance
subtitle: Equilibrium and missing support forces
paragraphs: A sign hanging at rest has forces acting on it. The reason it stays at rest is that those forces balance. Equilibrium means zero acceleration, so the force sum is zero in every direction. Today we will use that condition to find a missing force rather than assume every support carries an equal share.

The shorthand is <eq>Σ<var>F</var> = 0</eq>. Along a vertical axis, that means the upward forces total the downward forces. Along a horizontal axis, rightward and leftward totals must match. Balance in one direction does not automatically prove balance in another. We check each direction that has forces acting along it.

Compare the upward arrows in Section C. The diagram shows a 20 N sign supported by two vertical ropes. One pulls up with 8 N, and the other pulls up with 12 N. Their combined support is 8 N + 12 N = 20 N, matching the downward weight. The two ropes do not need equal tensions. Their sum needs to provide the required upward force.

The example in Section D uses a 40 N sign. It remains at rest, and one vertical rope has a tension of 15 N. Call the other tension T2. Because up equals down, 15 N + T2 = 40 N. Subtract the known support from the weight: T2 = 40 N − 15 N = 25 N upward.

Check the result by adding it back: <eq>15 N + 25 N − 40 N = 0 N</eq>. That agrees with zero acceleration. Dividing the weight equally between the ropes would have given 20 N each, but that would ignore the supplied 15 N tension. I want the given evidence, not a picture that merely looks symmetrical, to determine the calculation.

These ropes are vertical, so their entire tension acts upward. If the ropes were angled, only their vertical components would support the weight and we would need another step. Naming the directions keeps a simple balance rule from being used in a situation where it no longer applies directly.

Equilibrium can also describe an object moving with constant velocity. Zero net force means velocity does not change; it does not require the velocity to be zero. On the other hand, zero velocity at one instant does not prove equilibrium. A tossed object can be momentarily stopped at its highest point while gravity still gives it downward acceleration.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, balanced forces would mean constant velocity. They would not automatically bring the asteroid to a stop. Before assuming steady motion, we need a reason to believe the net force is zero or small enough for our chosen approximation. The force balance and the motion model should support the same explanation.

title: Repair the reasoning, not just the answer
subtitle: Finding the first mistake and checking the correction
paragraphs: When an answer is wrong, changing the final number does not explain what happened. I want us to find the first step where the reasoning stopped matching the situation. Then we can repair that step and follow the correction through the rest of the work. The pictures on today's notes page make four common mistakes visible.

Check the first strip in Section C. The claim confuses distance and displacement. A trip goes 3 m right and 3 m back. The total distance is 3 m + 3 m = 6 m. Displacement is 0 m because the starting and finishing positions match. A route sketch shows both facts: tracing the full path gives distance, while joining the endpoints gives displacement.

The second claim uses an applied force as if it were the net force. An 8 N pull acts on a 2 kg cart, with 2 N opposing it. Before dividing by mass, find Fnet = 8 N − 2 N = 6 N. Then a = 6 N ÷ 2 kg = 3 m/s². The missing subtraction was the first wrong step.

The third claim calls a change from −2 m/s to −6 m/s slowing down. The minus sign indicates direction. Speed is the size of velocity, so it grows from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. The object is speeding up in the negative direction. A velocity-time graph would move farther below zero; that does not mean its speed is getting smaller.

The fourth claim says a third-law pair cancels so nothing moves. Each member acts on a different object. Draw one force on each object's separate force diagram. They cannot cancel in the force sum for one receiver. If we combine both objects into one system, the pair is internal, but the objects can still change their motion relative to each other.

The example in Section D gives another force-sum repair. A 3 kg cart has 9 N right and 3 N left. Dividing the 9 N pull by mass ignores the other force. The correction is Fnet = 9 N − 3 N = 6 N right, followed by a = 6 N ÷ 3 kg = 2 m/s² right. Check backward: (3 kg)(2 m/s²) = 6 N, which matches the net force.

A useful explanation points to evidence and names a rule. The drawing can show a missing force, a return trip, or the receiver of an interaction. The equation then shows the correction. Keep units with the numbers and check whether the sign describes the chosen positive direction. Repeating the same mistaken substitution in another formula is not an independent check.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, one missed starting position or incorrect sign can affect every later prediction. Before trusting the forecast, trace it back through its evidence and model. Showing the first repaired step makes a revision understandable instead of leaving someone to guess why the final answer changed.

title: Connect the forces to the final position
subtitle: The complete chain from net force to a motion prediction
paragraphs: We have learned how forces change velocity and how velocity changes position. Today we connect those ideas in one calculation. I want you to keep the same object, positive direction, and time interval throughout the chain. Each result supplies information needed for the next step.

Follow the four links in Section C. The chain begins with a 2 kg cart at rest at 1 m. A 6 N pull acts right while 2 N of friction acts left. These forces stay constant for 2 s. Choose right as positive. First find Fnet = 6 N − 2 N = +4 N. Then a = Fnet ÷ m = 4 N ÷ 2 kg = 2 m/s².

The cart gains 2 m/s of velocity each second. Use <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>a</var><var>t</var></eq> to find <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = 0 m/s + (2 m/s²)(2 s) = +4 m/s</eq>. Constant net force on a fixed mass gives constant acceleration, so its velocity-time graph would be a straight rising line.

Because the acceleration is constant, average velocity is <eq>(0 + 4) m/s ÷ 2 = 2 m/s</eq>. Multiply by the two seconds to find <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = (2 m/s)(2 s) = +4 m</eq>. Now include the starting position: <eq><var>x</var><sub>f</sub> = 1 m + 4 m = 5 m</eq>. The cart's displacement is four meters, while its final position is the five-meter mark.

The diagram reports an illustrative bound of 5 ± 1 m, meaning a range from 4 m to 6 m. That one-meter bound is supplied for the example; it does not come from the force calculation alone. The center is not guaranteed to be the exact measured result, and the range is not a probability statement.

Section D tests a different case: a cart already moving at +2 m/s has zero net force for 3 s. Zero net force gives zero acceleration, so the velocity stays at +2 m/s. Its displacement is Δx = (2 m/s)(3 s) = +6 m. The cart keeps moving even though no unbalanced force acts on it.

Notice what information each step needs. Force and mass give acceleration. Starting velocity and time are needed to find final velocity. Starting position is needed to find final position. Orange identifies the force step, purple identifies velocity, and blue identifies position. Green in this particular diagram marks speeding up; acceleration itself does not always mean increasing speed.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, this chain connects the observations and interactions to a forecast. A force calculation alone is not the whole prediction. We also need the existing motion and starting location, along with a model that fits the interval being studied.

title: Make the situation clear before calculating
subtitle: A reference frame, useful evidence, and a prediction plan
paragraphs: A prediction begins with a situation, not a formula. Before calculating, I want us to identify where the object starts, how it moves, and what we need to find. A clear sketch and a short list of given values can prevent mistakes that are difficult to notice after several lines of arithmetic.

Choose a reference point and mark it as zero. Name the positive direction, or both axes if the motion is two-dimensional. Find the three features of the sketch in Section C: a reference point, a current location, and a motion arrow. Those features do different jobs. Blue identifies location, purple identifies motion, and the reference axes remain in pencil.

Copy each given quantity with its unit. A position in meters is different from a velocity in meters per second. Time must also use units that match the velocity or acceleration. Keeping each quantity on its own line makes it easier to see whether an equation uses all the information it needs.

Next choose a model and state its assumption. If velocity stays steady, use <eq><var>x</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>x</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>v</var><var>t</var></eq>. If constant acceleration changes velocity, <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>a</var><var>t</var></eq> describes that change. A position prediction under acceleration also needs an appropriate displacement step. Do not choose a steady-velocity model simply because it gives the shortest calculation.

The prediction in Section D gives a starting position of 2 m, a steady velocity of +3 m/s, and an elapsed time of 4 s. The question asks for final position. First find the change: Δx = (3 m/s)(4 s) = +12 m. Then add the start: xf = 2 m + 12 m = 14 m. Writing both steps makes it clear why the answer is not just 12 m.

Check the result against the story. Positive velocity should increase the coordinate. Four seconds at three meters per second should add twelve meters. Starting at two meters then places the object at fourteen meters. A number-line sketch can confirm both the direction and the size of that change. The units also reduce correctly to meters.

In two dimensions, solve the horizontal and vertical coordinates separately using the corresponding velocity components and the same elapsed time. Do not use the whole diagonal speed as if it were the speed along each axis. If the evidence includes a prediction range, read its lower and upper limits before making a claim; the central value alone does not describe the whole result.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, the plan connects relevant measurements to a stated model. A classroom model may treat Earth as a fixed reference and velocity as steady over a chosen interval. Those are assumptions to explain and check. A defensible plan shows how the evidence can answer where the asteroid will be at a particular future time without claiming information the measurements do not provide.

title: Explain what the forecast means and what limits it
subtitle: Claim, evidence, reasoning, and a visible revision
paragraphs: A correct-looking number is not the same as shown reasoning. Someone reading a forecast needs to know what was predicted, which evidence supports it, and what assumptions connect the two. Today I want the explanation to be clear enough that another person could follow the calculation and understand its limits.

Follow the parts of the defense in Section C. A claim states the result. Evidence is the visible work supporting it: measurements, a graph, a sketch, or a calculation. Reasoning explains why the physics model connects that evidence to the claim. A limitation identifies something uncertain, assumed, or left out. These four parts work together rather than replacing one another.

The forecast in Section D uses a 2 kg cart under a constant 4 N net force. It starts at rest at 1 m, and we predict its position after 2 s. First find a = 4 N ÷ 2 kg = 2 m/s². Then vf = 0 m/s + (2 m/s²)(2 s) = 4 m/s. The constant net force and fixed mass justify constant acceleration.

Average velocity is (0 + 4) m/s ÷ 2 = 2 m/s, so Δx = (2 m/s)(2 s) = 4 m. Add the starting coordinate: xf = 1 m + 4 m = 5 m. The example supplies a model bound of ±1 m, so the reported position interval is 4 m to 6 m. The bound is part of the supplied information, not something this arithmetic creates by itself.

A defense can now connect the pieces: we predict a central position of 5 m after two seconds, with the given range from 4 m to 6 m. The evidence is the force, mass, starting conditions, and time. The reasoning uses Newton's second law and constant-acceleration motion. The result is limited by the supplied bound and the assumption that the forces stay constant throughout the interval.

A range is not a probability. This example does not tell us that some percentage of outcomes must occur inside it. Also, a model can miss a changing force even when its arithmetic is correct. I want uncertainty in the inputs and limits of the model named honestly, rather than hidden behind extra decimal places.

A revision should show the corrected step and its effect on later results. For example, if the starting coordinate were corrected from 1 m to 2 m, with everything else unchanged, the displacement would still be 4 m but the central final position would become <eq>2 m + 4 m = 6 m</eq>. We can explain exactly why that result changed instead of simply replacing the old answer.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a useful forecast includes a location, future time, reference frame, supporting work, and limits. Decisions about a response also involve cost, feasibility, and priorities. Physics supplies evidence for those decisions. A clear defense shows what the model supports and what additional information people still need.
